newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European insurance market still far from a reality.
newsitem.headline: European insurance market still far from a reality.

text.p: Three years after European Union laws gave insurance companies the right to operate throughout the bloc with a single licence, a European insurance market is still far from reality .
The European Insurance Committee (CEA), which represents the industry across Europe, said on Thursday the market was still largely divided along national lines.
For that reason companies still favoured opening local branches and subsidiaries rather than operating directly from their domestic market.
Different tax regimes, widespread discriminatory measures under the cover of the 'general good' concept and language problems were some of the barriers invoked.

"An insurer must be close to its customers," CEA secretary general Francis Loheac told a news conference called to present a manual to help operators take advantage of the single market for life insurance while avoiding its pitfalls.
The EU insurance single market, which recorded global premiums of 455 billion European currency units ($512 billion) in 1996, was theoretically completed on July 1, 1994.

This means that an insurer duly authorised in any of the EU's 15 states and Norway, Iceland and Lichtenstein -- in what forms the European Economic Area -- can market all its products throughout Europe under the control of its domestic supervising body only.
CEA said the EU's vast and complex legislation described in the manual had done much to cut national red tape and to deregulate at all levels including rates and distribution channels.

Since the advent of the single market, insurance firms no longer have to submit to a cumbersome and systematic prior examination of their contracts and tariffs before they can operate outside their country.
But problems remain and the lack of a common tax regime is one of the biggest.

Currently many EU states do not grant tax incentives on certain insurance premiums which are paid elsewhere. This usually discourages individuals from shopping abroad for a cheaper life insurance unless the benefits outweigh the costs.
Many people living in Belgium have made the calculation and found that it is worth investing in attractive, anonymous, life products in Luxembourg which are free of rights of succession.
"Life insurance has considerably developed in Luxembourg due to tax reasons," Loheac said adding: "We must move towards tax harmonisation if we want to have fair and healthy competition."

He was hopeful that the advent of the euro, the future European single currency, would help achieve greater coordination on tax matters which have so far been deadlocked by the need for unanimous agreement among EU states. $1 = 0.887 Ecus
